q: Your organisation is starting a PAM programme with roughly 40,000 privileged accounts. Following CyberArk's recommended discovery-and-initiation approach, which accounts should be secured first?
opts: Workstation local administrator accounts, because there are the most of them
Tier 0 accounts — Domain and Forest Admins, the Vault / Privilege Cloud administrators, and the hypervisor platform hosting them
Application and service accounts embedded in scripts
Third-party vendor accounts
why: Tier 0 is the set of accounts that control the identity infrastructure itself. If a Domain Admin, a Vault admin or the hypervisor running the Domain Controllers is compromised, every other control in the environment is bypassable — so these are secured in Phase 1 (Discovery and initiation). Domain Controllers are always classified as critical.
wrong: A = Tier 2 (workstation admins), addressed in later phases. C and D matter a great deal, but neither hands an attacker the whole directory the way Tier 0 does. The tiering model is Tier 0 / 1 / 2 only — there is no Tier 3.
ref: PAM Implementation Program Phase 1 — Discovery and initiation

q: You are configuring a UNIX Accounts Discovery. Besides the CSV list of machines, you must supply a UNIX user name and password. What is that credential used for?
opts: It becomes the reconcile account for every account that is discovered
It is the credential the CPM Scanner uses to log on to each machine in the CSV list and enumerate local accounts and SSH keys
It is the password that will be set on all discovered accounts when they are onboarded
It authenticates the scanner to the Vault
why: UNIX discovery has no directory to read, so CyberArk needs a way in to each host. The CSV supplies the targets and the supplied UNIX account supplies the login used to enumerate `/etc/passwd`, local accounts and SSH keys on each one.
wrong: A — the reconcile account is defined on the platform or per account, not by the scan. C — discovery never changes passwords; that is the CPM's job after onboarding. D — the scanner authenticates to the Vault with its own component credential file, not this account.

q: Three onboarding rules already exist. You create a fourth. A newly discovered account matches both your new rule and rule #2. Which rule is applied?
opts: Rule #2 — older rules take priority because they were established first
The new rule — it is created with precedence 1, and an account is onboarded by the first rule it matches
Both rules run, and the account is onboarded into both Safes
Neither; the conflict sends the account to the Pending Accounts list
why: Precedence is based on creation time and runs newest-first: the most recently created rule gets precedence 1, the next most recent gets 2, and so on. A discovered account is compared against precedence 1 first, and the first rule it matches wins. This is counter-intuitive and a favourite exam trap.
wrong: A inverts the real order. C — an account is onboarded once, by one rule. D — accounts only land in Pending when *no* rule matches.

q: An onboarding rule targets a Safe called WIN-SRV-ADMINS, which does not exist in the Vault. What happens when a matching account is discovered?
opts: The Safe is created automatically with default properties
Nothing is onboarded — the target Safe (and the reconcile account, if the rule references one) must exist before the rule can run
The accounts go to PasswordManager_Pending and the Safe is created on first onboarding
The CPM creates the Safe but leaves it unmanaged
why: Onboarding rules place accounts into existing containers; they do not provision them. The documented prerequisites are to create the Safe and the reconcile account according to the rule's definition first, and the rule's author must be a member of the target Safe with Add Account permission.
wrong: A and C both assume auto-creation, which does not happen. D invents behaviour the CPM does not have.

q: Which two statements about "Add multiple accounts from a file" (bulk upload) are correct? (Choose two)
opts: Each file can contain a maximum of 10,000 accounts
Safes and account groups referenced in the file are created automatically if they are missing
All accounts must be uploaded into Safes and groups that already exist
Only XLSX files are supported
why: The documented ceiling is 10,000 accounts per file, and the upload writes only into Safes and account groups that already exist — it is a loading mechanism, not a provisioning mechanism.
wrong: B is the opposite of the documented behaviour. D is wrong: only CSV is supported, and the first row must be a header row of property names. A sample CSV template can be downloaded from the Add accounts from file window.
ref: Add multiple accounts from a file

q: A bulk upload of 4,000 accounts finishes with 63 failures. How do you find out which rows failed and why?
opts: Read pm_error.log on the CPM
Download the failed-accounts CSV that the PVWA produces — it returns the failed rows with two extra columns, Errors and uploadIndex
Check ITALog.log on the Vault
Re-run the upload; only the failed rows are retried automatically
why: The PVWA gives you back a CSV containing only the failed rows, annotated with `Errors` (the reason) and `uploadIndex` (the row's position in the original file). You fix that file and re-upload it.
wrong: A and C are component logs — the failures here are data validation, not a component fault. D — nothing is retried automatically; the re-upload is a manual action.
ref: Add multiple accounts from a file / Create bulk upload of accounts (REST)

q: A content administrator adds an account for srv-app01\svc_backup in the PVWA. What has happened on the target server?
opts: A new local account named svc_backup has been created on srv-app01
Nothing — adding an account registers information about an account that already exists; it does not provision anything on the target
The account's password has already been rotated
The account has been added to the local Administrators group
why: "Add account" is a Vault-side registration: it records the address, username, platform and current password so CyberArk can start managing an account that is already there. This is one of the most commonly misunderstood points on the exam.
wrong: A — CyberArk never creates target accounts as part of onboarding. C — a change only happens if the platform or the operator triggers one afterwards. D — group membership is never altered by onboarding.

q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between an account, a Safe and a platform?
opts: An account can live in several Safes but is associated with only one platform
Every account is stored in exactly one Safe and associated with exactly one target account platform
An account can be linked to several target platforms so that different CPMs can manage it
The platform determines which Safe the account is stored in
why: One Safe, one target account platform — always. The Safe controls who can reach the account and which CPM manages it; the platform controls how it is managed. Both are mandatory and singular.
wrong: A and C break the one-to-one rule. D reverses the relationship: the Safe is chosen at onboarding, and it is the Safe (not the platform) that carries the CPM assignment.

q: A Windows Accounts Discovery has finished. On what basis does it mark a discovered local account as Privileged?
opts: The account name begins with "admin"
The account is a member of a local Administrators group on at least one scanned machine
The account has a non-expiring password
The account has logged on within the last 30 days
why: Categorisation is by group membership. Membership of any local Administrators group on any scanned machine makes the account privileged, and it stays privileged until it has been removed from that group on every machine it was discovered on.
wrong: A — naming is a keyword filter you can use in an onboarding rule, not the categorisation basis. C and D are account attributes discovery records but does not categorise on.

q: Which of the following can a Windows Accounts Discovery detect as a dependency? (Choose three)
opts: Windows Services
Scheduled Tasks
IIS Application Pools
A connection string inside a web.config file
why: Discovery finds dependencies that are registered in a machine's own configuration surface: Windows services, scheduled tasks, IIS application pools, IIS anonymous access and COM+ applications. It can read those programmatically.
wrong: D — credentials sitting inside arbitrary text, XML, INI or web configuration files, database connection strings, registry keys and private SSH keys cannot be discovered. The CPM can *manage* them once you add them by hand, but it cannot find them.

q: A Windows discovery completes but returns only machine names — no local accounts. The scan account is a domain user with read access to Active Directory. What is missing?
opts: The scan account needs Domain Admin
The scan account needs local administrative rights on the scanned servers and workstations
The CPM needs the Backup All Safes authorization
Discovery must be run from the PVWA server rather than the CPM
why: Windows discovery runs in two phases. Phase 1 reads the directory to build the list of machines in the specified OU — AD read access is enough for that, which is why you got machine names. Phase 2 connects to each machine and enumerates its local accounts and dependencies, and that requires local administrative rights on the target.
wrong: A — Domain Admin is over-privileged and is not required. C — that is a Vault backup authorization, unrelated. D — the scan is always executed by the CPM Scanner.
ref: Accounts Discovery — Windows, scan account permissions

q: Which statement about running an Accounts Discovery is correct?
opts: The PVWA runs the scan and writes results directly into the Vault
The CPM Scanner runs the scan; it is configured in the PVWA, and the CPM must be able to reach the PVWA on TCP 443
PTA runs the scan by analysing network traffic
The PrivateArk Client runs the scan
why: Discovery is defined in the PVWA but executed by the CPM Scanner service on the CPM machine. Because the scanner pulls its configuration from and reports back through the PVWA's web services, CPM → PVWA on 443 is a hard prerequisite — a missing firewall rule here is the classic "discovery never starts" cause.
wrong: A — the PVWA only holds the definition. C — PTA does continuous *detection* of newly privileged accounts from AD/network telemetry, which is a different mechanism. D — the PrivateArk Client is an administration interface, not a scanner.

q: A UNIX discovery has finished. Which of these can it bring back in addition to local accounts?
opts: SSH keys found on the scanned machines, including authorized and trusted keys
Oracle database accounts on those machines
cron jobs that use the discovered accounts
sudoers entries
why: UNIX discovery enumerates local accounts *and* SSH keys, including the authorized/trusted key relationships between machines — which is often the more valuable half of the result, because key-based trust paths are how attackers move laterally across a UNIX estate.
wrong: B — database accounts live inside the database, not the OS account store, and need their own onboarding. C and D — cron and sudoers are not discoverable dependency types.
ref: Accounts Discovery — UNIX / onboard SSH keys

q: You are onboarding an account from the Pending Accounts list onto a platform that requires a reconcile account. What must be true?
opts: The reconcile account must already be stored in a Safe and be referenced by the platform (or specified on the account)
The CPM creates the reconcile account automatically during onboarding
Reconcile accounts are only required for UNIX accounts
The reconcile account must be stored in the same Safe as the account being onboarded
why: A reconcile account is just another vaulted account. It has to exist and be reachable before the platform can use it — which is why "create the Safe and the reconcile account first" is a documented prerequisite for onboarding rules as well.
wrong: B — nothing is auto-created. C — reconciliation applies to Windows, UNIX, databases and appliances alike. D — the reconcile account can sit in a dedicated Safe; the platform's ReconcileAccountSafe setting exists precisely so it does not have to share the Safe.
ref: Onboard accounts from the pending accounts list

q: You have limited onboarding capacity this quarter. Which of these should be onboarded first?
opts: A shared read-only monitoring account present on 200 Linux hosts
The break-glass local Administrator account on every Domain Controller
A developer's personal named account on a test server
An FTP service account used by a nightly reporting job
why: Prioritisation is risk-based, not volume-based. The local Administrator on a Domain Controller is Tier 0: it grants control of the machine that holds the directory, and it is the classic persistence and escalation target.
wrong: A is high-volume but low-privilege — impressive onboarding statistics, minimal risk reduction. C is a named low-privilege account on a non-production box. D matters but is a Tier 1/2 service account. Volume and ease are the wrong prioritisation criteria.

q: A colleague copies user.ini from CPM-01 to a new CPM-02 to save time. CPM-02 cannot authenticate to the Vault. Why?
opts: The credential file is bound to the machine that created it — CreateCredFile.exe hardens it with machine-specific data such as /IpAddress, /Hostname and /EntropyFile
Credential files expire after 24 hours
The Vault rejects any credential file that is not listed in Vault.ini
The file has to be renamed to cpm.cred on a second CPM
why: A credential file is not a portable secret. When it is generated you bind it to the host with parameters such as `/IpAddress`, `/Hostname` and `/EntropyFile`, so the Vault will only accept it when presented from that machine. A new component gets its own Vault user and its own freshly generated credential file.
wrong: B is true of the Privilege Cloud `installeruser` password, not of credential files. C — Vault.ini holds the Vault's address and port, nothing about credential files. D — file naming is irrelevant to the failure.

q: Which of these does NOT open its own session to the Vault over port 1858?
opts: CPM
PVWA
The PSM HTML5 Gateway
PTA
why: The HTML5 Gateway sits between the user's browser and the PSM. The browser reaches it over a secure WebSocket on 443, and it connects onward to the PSM server over RDP. It never authenticates to the Vault and holds no Vault credential of its own.
wrong: The CPM, PVWA, PSM and PTA all authenticate to the Vault with their own component users over the CyberArk proprietary protocol on 1858 (which can be moved to 443).
ref: PSM HTML5 Gateway architecture / component ports

q: Which is the correct 2nd-generation REST logon endpoint for LDAP authentication?
opts: https://<PVWA>/PasswordVault/API/auth/LDAP/Logon/
https://<PVWA>/PasswordVault/WebServices/auth/LDAP/Logon
https://<PVWA>/API/LDAP/Authenticate
https://<Vault>:1858/API/auth/LDAP/Logon
why: The 2nd-generation API base path is `https://<PVWA_Server_address>/PasswordVault/API/`, and the logon endpoints follow the pattern `auth/<method>/Logon/` for Cyberark, LDAP, Windows and RADIUS.
wrong: B is the 1st-generation (legacy) path under /WebServices/ — still documented, but not the recommended one. C is not a CyberArk path. D is wrong on two counts: the REST API is served by the PVWA over HTTPS, not by the Vault on 1858.

q: Your identity team wants new joiners' Safe memberships created automatically by their joiner/mover/leaver workflow. What is the appropriate mechanism?
opts: A scheduled PARestore job
The PAM REST API — it exposes the operations normally performed by hand in the PVWA so they can be scripted and embedded in provisioning automation
The Remote Control Client
A nightly EVD export
why: That is exactly the stated purpose of the REST API: to automate tasks that are usually performed manually through the interface, so they can be driven from provisioning scripts, ITSM tools and CI/CD pipelines.
wrong: A is a Vault restore utility. C administers Vault services remotely on 9022. D exports audit data outward — none of them write configuration into the Vault.

q: By default, how long does a PAM REST API authentication token remain valid?
opts: 5 minutes
20 minutes
1 hour
It never expires until an explicit Logoff call is made
why: A REST session token is valid for 20 minutes by default. Long-running automation must either finish inside that window or re-authenticate; well-behaved scripts also call Logoff so the session is released rather than left to time out.
wrong: D is a common wrong assumption — Logoff is good practice, but the token expires on its own regardless.

q: A firewall team asks which single port must be open from the CPM, PVWA and PSM servers to the Vault. What do you tell them?
opts: TCP 443
TCP 1858 — the CyberArk proprietary Vault protocol
TCP 9022
TCP 3389
why: Every component talks to the Vault over the CyberArk proprietary protocol on TCP 1858 (it can be reconfigured to 443). DR replication, PAReplicate backups, EVD and PTA all use the same channel.
wrong: 443 is what *users* use to reach the PVWA, and what the CPM needs to reach the PVWA for Accounts Discovery — but it is not the component-to-Vault port by default. 9022 is Remote Control Client → PARAgent. 3389 is RDP.

q: Which dbparm.ini setting pair controls how long a component may be silent before the Vault treats it as inactive and raises a notification?
opts: ComponentMonitoringInterval together with ComponentNotificationThreshold
MonitorFWRulesInterval
AutoSyncExternalObjects
UserLockoutPeriodInMinutes
why: `ComponentMonitoringInterval` sets how often the Vault checks component activity; `ComponentNotificationThreshold` takes the form `CPM, Yes, 720, 1440` — component, notify or not, minutes before the first notification, minutes between subsequent ones. The resulting message uses notification template 206, "Component is inactive".
wrong: B governs the periodic ITATS319W firewall-rules message. C controls LDAP object synchronisation. D auto-unsuspends locked-out users.

q: An administrator cannot find anywhere in the PVWA to grant the "Audit Users" authorization. Why not?
opts: It was removed in version 12
Vault-level authorizations are managed only in the PrivateArk Client; the PVWA manages Safe-level permissions
Only the Master user can see it
It is a Master Policy rule, not an authorization
why: There are two distinct permission planes. Vault-level authorizations (Add Safes, Audit Users, Manage Users, Backup All Safes, Restore All Safes…) are assigned to individual users in the PrivateArk Client and are not inherited through groups. Safe-level permissions are granted to users or groups, and are inherited — those are what the PVWA exposes.
wrong: A is false. C — Administrator and other privileged users can set them too. D confuses authorizations with policy rules.

q: Where is the CyberArk licence stored, and how is it updated?
opts: In dbparm.ini; a Vault restart is required
As License.xml in the System Safe — a new file can be copied in without restarting the Vault
In the PVWAConfig Safe; IIS must be restarted afterwards
On the CyberArk Marketplace; the Vault fetches it hourly
why: The licence lives as `License.xml` inside the `System` Safe. Copying in a replacement file updates the licence in place, which is why licence renewals do not require a maintenance window.
wrong: A — dbparm.ini holds Vault configuration, and any change there *does* need a restart, which is part of why this distractor is tempting. C is the PVWA's configuration Safe. D is invented.

q: You need to check and restart the PrivateArk Server service from a remote administration station. Which mechanism, and over which port?
opts: The Remote Control Client talking to the Remote Control Agent (PARAgent) over TCP 9022
RDP on 3389
PACLI on 1858
SSH on 22
why: The Vault Remote Control feature is a pair: the PARAgent service on the Vault and the Remote Control Client on the administration station, communicating on TCP 9022. From the client you run commands such as `status vault`, `stop vault`, `start vault`, `status ene`.
wrong: B — a hardened Vault should not accept RDP. C — PACLI is a command-line interface for Vault *data*, not for service control. D — the Windows Vault does not run SSH.

q: pm.log on the CPM repeatedly shows ITATS004E Password authentication failed, and System Health shows the CPM as Disconnected. What is the correct fix?
opts: Restart the PrivateArk Server service on the Vault

Stop the CPM services, reset the PasswordManager user's password in the PrivateArk Client, activate (unsuspend) the user, regenerate the credential file with CreateCredFile.exe using the same password, then start the services
Re-run the PSM hardening script
Raise CPMDebugLevels to 6 and wait
why: This is the classic out-of-sync component user. The credential file rotates the component's password on every successful logon, so if the file and the Vault ever diverge — a restored VM snapshot, a copied file, a failed rotation — authentication fails and repeated failures suspend the user. The fix must do all four things in order: stop, reset, unsuspend, rebuild the credential file, start.
wrong: A — if the Vault service were down, *every* component would be disconnected, not just the CPM. C is unrelated to Vault authentication. D increases logging but fixes nothing.

q: A single Oracle account fails to change while every other account on the same CPM is fine. Which log will tell you why?
opts: pm_error.log
The per-plugin log under Logs\ThirdParty\, named <type>-<Safe>-<folder>-<object>.log
PMConsole.log
ITALog.log
why: The CPM writes a separate log per managed object under `Logs\ThirdParty\`, named after the plugin type, Safe, folder and object. When one account misbehaves and the rest are healthy, that per-object log is where the plugin's actual conversation with the target is recorded. Uploaded copies are kept under `Logs\History\`.
wrong: A gives you warnings and errors across the whole CPM — useful for spotting the failure, not for diagnosing it. C is console output. D is the Vault's log and knows nothing about an Oracle plugin.

q: Where do the PVWA application logs live by default?
opts: %windir%\temp — the location is set by LogFolder in web.config
C:\Program Files\CyberArk\PVWA\Logs
Inside the PVWAReports Safe
/var/opt/CARKpvwa/logs
why: By default the PVWA writes CyberArk.WebApplication.log, CyberArk.WebConsole.log and per-session CyberArk.WebSession.<id>.log into `%windir%\temp`, controlled by the `LogFolder` setting in web.config. Many sites move this, so always check web.config before hunting.
wrong: B looks plausible but is not the default. C holds generated reports, not logs. D is a Linux path — the PVWA is an IIS application on Windows.

q: PSM for SSH connections are failing. Which logs do you check, and where?
opts: PSMConsole.log in C:\Program Files\CyberArk\PSM\Logs
PSMPConsole.log and PSMPTrace.log in /var/opt/CARKPSMP/logs/
pm.log and pm_error.log on the CPM
ITALog.log and Trace.d0 on the Vault
why: PSM for SSH (PSMP) is a Linux component with its own log set: `PSMPConsole.log` and `PSMPTrace.log` under `/var/opt/CARKPSMP/logs/`. Its configuration lives in `/etc/opt/CARKPSMP/conf/basic_PSMPserver.conf`, and the service is controlled with `/etc/init.d/psmpsrv`.
wrong: A is the Windows PSM, a different component. C is the CPM. D is the Vault.

q: Which of the following is a services engagement rather than a break/fix support case?
opts: A PSM session fails to launch after a Windows update
Designing and building a custom CPM plugin for an unsupported in-house application
A component user is suspended after repeated failed logons
The DR Vault has stopped replicating
why: Break/fix is restoring documented, expected behaviour of a supported product. Building something that does not exist yet — a custom plugin, a new Safe model, an architecture design — is professional services work, because there is no "working state" to restore.
wrong: A, C and D are all documented failure modes of supported functionality with documented remediation procedures, which makes them support cases.

q: You edit DebugLevel in dbparm.ini on the Vault. When does the change take effect?
opts: Immediately — the Vault re-reads dbparm.ini every minute
After the PrivateArk Server service is restarted; dbparm.ini changes always require a Vault restart
After 20 minutes, on the next configuration refresh
Only after the next full backup
why: `dbparm.ini` is read at service start. Any change to it — DebugLevel, Syslog, firewall rules, thresholds — needs a restart of the PrivateArk Server service. Two supporting files help here: `dbparm.sample.ini` lists every available option, and `dbparm.ini.good` is written automatically after a successful start so you have a known-good copy to fall back to.
wrong: A and C describe the PVWA's periodic configuration refresh, not the Vault. D is unrelated. Note that the Vault Server Central Administration Station can change the debug level without a restart — which is exactly why that tool exists.

q: CyberArk Support asks for a log bundle. Which statement is correct?
opts: Run CAVaultManager CollectLogs on the Vault; xRay is the broader tool that collects encrypted logs and configuration from PAM components and is downloaded from the CyberArk Marketplace
Run PARestore.exe /CollectLogs
Export the data with EVD and send the CSV
Copy ITALog.log — Support only needs the Vault's main log
why: `CAVaultManager CollectLogs` gathers the Vault's own logs. xRay is the general-purpose diagnostic collector across PAM components — it packages logs and configuration files in encrypted form for Support, and you get it from the CyberArk Marketplace, not from the installation media.
wrong: B — PARestore restores Safes from backup. C — EVD exports audit *data* for reporting, not diagnostics. D is almost never sufficient; Support needs configuration alongside logs.

q: After a new database client is installed on a PSM server, sessions that use it fail immediately. What is the most likely cause and fix?
opts: The recording Safe is full — raise MaxSafeSize
AppLocker has no rule for the new executable — add it to PSMConfigureAppLocker.xml and re-run PSMConfigureApplocker.ps1
Network Level Authentication must be disabled on the PSM
The connection component must be deleted and recreated
why: PSM hardening puts AppLocker in place so only explicitly permitted binaries can run in a PSM session. Any new client application is blocked until it is whitelisted — you add it to `PSMConfigureAppLocker.xml` and re-run `PSMConfigureApplocker.ps1`. "It worked in testing before hardening" is the tell.
wrong: A would show as an upload failure after the session, not an instant launch failure. C and D do not produce an immediate application-launch block.

q: PSM sessions fail with a logon-rights error for the shadow user PSM-jdoe. What should you check?
opts: That the PSMShadowUsers local group still holds the "Allow log on locally" right — hardening or a domain GPO can strip it
That jdoe has been added to the Auditors group
That PSMConnect has been converted to a domain account
That the Vault firewall permits 3389
why: For non-RDP-file connections the PSM auto-creates a local shadow user `PSM-<userid>` per Vault user, with credentials reset on every connection. Those users sit in the local `PSMShadowUsers` group, which must retain the "Allow log on locally" user right. A tightening GPO applied after PSM hardening is the usual culprit.
wrong: B is about auditing, not session logon. C is not a supported change. D would break the connection before any logon error appeared.

q: The CPM cannot change a local Windows account's password; the target rejects the new value. The platform generates 12-character passwords. What do you check first?
opts: Whether the target's local or group password policy — complexity, minimum length, password history, minimum password age — conflicts with the platform's password policy
Whether the Vault has spare licence capacity
Whether the account has been added to the Auditors group
Whether SearchForUsages is enabled on the platform
why: When the target itself rejects the password, the mismatch is almost always between the platform's generated password policy and what the operating system will accept. Minimum password *age* is the sneakiest of these: it silently blocks a second change within the same day, which looks like an intermittent failure.
wrong: B would prevent onboarding, not changing. C is unrelated. D controls dependency scanning after a successful change.

q: You see ITATS310E in a log. What can you infer before looking it up?
opts: It came from the PVWA and is informational
It originated on the Vault server (the ITA prefix) and the trailing E marks it as an Error
It came from the CPM and is a System message
It is a PSM warning
why: CyberArk message codes are readable at a glance. The leading letters identify the originating component and module — `ITA…` means the Vault server — and the trailing letter is the category: I = Informational, W = Warning, E = Error, S = System.
wrong: The other options mis-read either the prefix or the suffix. Practise this: ITADB367S is a Vault database System message; ITATS319W is a Vault warning.

q: A Vault user is suspended after five failed logon attempts. Which two are valid ways to restore access? (Choose two)
opts: Activate the user in the PrivateArk Client under Users and Groups
Wait for the period set by UserLockoutPeriodInMinutes in dbparm.ini to elapse, where it is configured
Restart the PrivateArk Server service
Delete the user in the PVWA and recreate them
why: Suspension is cleared either manually — an administrator activates the user in the PrivateArk Client — or automatically, if `UserLockoutPeriodInMinutes` is set in dbparm.ini, after which the Vault unsuspends the user itself.
wrong: C does not clear a suspension. D is destructive: deleting a user loses their individually-assigned Safe permissions, which is one of the strongest arguments for granting permissions to groups rather than to people.
